judgments.title: MUHAMMAD RASUL BIN MAHAZIR v Pendakwa Raya & ors
judgments.catchwords: CRIMINAL LAW — Dangerous Drugs — Self-administration of dangerous drugs — s 15(1)(a) Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 — Urine specimen — Chain of evidence — Failure to record precise time of sealing — Whether giving rise to reasonable doubt — Specimen duly collected, sealed, handed over and analysed — Chain of custody established by oral and documentary evidence — No evidence of contamination or tampering — s 31A of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952— Alleged non-compliance in taking urine specimen — Whether occasioning prejudice — Appellant’s defence rejected — Credibility of prosecution witness —No material irregularity or prejudice — Conviction and sentence upheld — Appeal dismissed. Held, dismissing the Appellant’s appeal: The Appellant appealed against his conviction under s 15(1)(a) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 for self-administration of cannabis. The Appellant contended that the prosecution failed to establish the chain of custody because the exact time of sealing the urine specimen was not recorded, and alleged that a second specimen had been provided at the District Police Headquarters. He further argued that the failure to record a potential witness’s statement prejudiced his defence. The Court found that the specimen’s collection, sealing, handover, storage and analysis were adequately established through oral and contemporaneous documentary evidence. No actual contamination or prejudice was demonstrated. The appeal was dismissed.

judgments.title: Pendakwa Raya & ors v Julasiri Bin Akilmara
judgments.catchwords: Offence under section 39B(1)(a) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 read together with section 34 of the Penal Code - Whether the trial judge should have informed at the close of the prosecution's case, that the defence was being called upon to answer a case of actual trafficking or presumed trafficking? - Overwhelming evidence proved the elements of custody, control, and knowledge - Actual possession of the impugned drugs was established - Section 180 (1) and (4) of the Criminal Procedure Code - Procedure after conclusion of case for prosecution - No statutory or legal requirement to state the presumption when calling for the defence - Formal verbal label for an evidentiary rule at the close of the prosecution's case is unnecessary - Statutory presumption of trafficking under section 37(da)(xvi) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 - Section 422 of the Criminal Procedure Code - Not vitiate the conviction - No miscarriage of justice - Failure either to make or to record such a finding does not ipso facto - The law does not require a mini-judgment or detailed legal reasons at the close of the prosecution’s case

judgments.catchwords: (1)(a) when a criminal appeal is lodged by the Public Prosecutor (PP) to the Court of Appeal against a decision of the High Court which concerns more than one accused person (Appeal); (b) one accused person (X) could not be present in the Court of Appeal even though the Court of Appeal has conducted previous mentions and/or case management (CM) for the Appeal; and (c) the co-accused person (Y) is present in the Court of Appeal and the PP has a discretion to proceed with the Appeal against Y only but the PP does not choose to do so - does the Court of Appeal have a discretion to strike out the Appeal pursuant to the second limb of r 105 (to prevent an abuse of process of the Court of Appeal) of the Rules of the Court of Appeal 1994 (RCA)?; and (2) if the Court of Appeal strikes out the Appeal [Court of Appeal’s Decision (Striking Out of Appeal)] - (a) can the PP subsequently apply to the Court of Appeal to reinstate the Appeal under the first limb of r 105 RCA (to prevent injustice) read with r 1A RCA, so as proceed with the Appeal against - (i) Y only; or (ii) X and Y; and (b) in view of the definition of “decision” in s 3 of the Courts of Judicature Act 1964 (CJA) and s 87(1) CJA, can the PP appeal to the Federal Court against the Court of Appeal’s Decision (Striking Out of Appeal)?

judgments.title: MAPLE AMALGAMATED SDN BHD (DALAM PENYELESAIAN) v LIM CHENG POW & ors

parties.label: DEFENDAN
names: LIEW HON KONG @ LIEW KWAN VOON
LEE SIAH SIAN @ LEE HAY HIAN

judgments.catchwords: The Plaintiff, a wound-up company suing through its court-appointed liquidator, alleged a conspiracy to defraud it via a sham management agreement over a palm oil estate. Several Defendants sought security for costs under s. 580A of the Companies Act 2016. The Court held the threshold satisfied — the Plaintiff's liquidation, an unpaid costs order and the absence of any contributory able to assist being credible testimony of inability to pay. The burden having shifted, the Plaintiff discharged it: its impecuniosity was materially contributed to by the very Defendants seeking security, the liquidator performs a public function, and the sums sought would stifle a genuine claim. Applications dismissed with costs. CIVIL PROCEDURE: Security for costs — Company in liquidation — Credible testimony of inability to pay — Shifting of burden — Impecuniosity caused by defendants seeking security — Whether oppressive — Companies Act 2016, s. 580A — Rules of Court 2012, O. 23 r. 1 COMPANY LAW: Winding up — Court-appointed liquidator performing public function — Conspiracy and breach of fiduciary duty — Merits not examined at interlocutory stage
judgments.judge: YA Puan Arziah binti Mohamed Apandi

judgments.title: SIVACHANDRAN A/L S JAYARAJAH v Pendakwa Raya
judgments.catchwords: Review jurisdiction - Rule 137 of the Rules of the Federal Court 1995 -Inherent powers of Federal Court – All sentences passed to be in accordance with the law – Avoiding miscarriage of justice - Exceptional circumstances - Fresh evidence of prisoner’s death following whipping. Constitutional Law - Federal Constitution - Articles 5(1), 8(1) and 8(2) Fundamental liberties - Life and personal liberty - Human dignity - Equal protection of the law - Whether it is in violation of medical ethics for medical officer to be participate in the execution of whipping. Judicial whipping - Corporal punishment - Whether judicial whipping amounts to cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment (“CIDT”) - Whether punishment of whipping is inconsistent with constitutional protection of life, dignity and bodily integrity. Whether whipping is disproportionate and therefore contrary to Article 8(1) - Whether exemption of women from whipping constitutes prohibited discrimination on ground only of gender is contrary to Art 8(2) - Intelligible differentia. Whether whipping is against Art. 5 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (“UDHR”) and the ASEAN Human Rights Declaration in its prohibitions against CIDT - Whether whipping is against customary international law.
